cards.front: Qualified account
cards.back: A retirement savings account that qualifies for tax-deferred growth. Some require employer sponsorship; IRAs are self-sponsored and not technically 'qualified' by the IRS but follow similar rules.

cards.front: What type of income must be used to make IRA contributions?
cards.back: Earned income (salary, wages, tips). Contributions cannot come from ordinary income items such as dividends, interest, or capital gains.

cards.front: By when must IRA contributions for a given tax year be made?
cards.back: By the first tax filing deadline of the following year (normally April 15). No extensions apply to contribution deadlines.

cards.front: Is there an age limit for making IRA contributions?
cards.back: No. There is no age limit for contributing to either a traditional or Roth IRA, provided the contributor has earned income.

cards.front: When is a traditional IRA contribution fully tax deductible?
cards.back: When the individual is not actively participating in another qualified plan (such as a 401(k)). If covered by another plan, deductibility phases out as AGI rises, but nondeductible contributions may still be made and grow tax deferred.

cards.front: Which investments and strategies are NOT permitted inside an IRA?
cards.back: Collectibles (antiques, gems, rare coins, art, stamps), life insurance, short sales, speculative options, margin trading, and municipal (tax-exempt) bonds. Covered call writing IS permitted as a conservative income strategy.

cards.front: Are annuities permitted inside an IRA?
cards.back: Yes, annuities are allowed inside an IRA, though FINRA has raised suitability concerns about placing a tax-favored product inside a tax-favored account.

cards.front: IRA rollover
cards.back: When a customer takes possession of IRA assets and redeposits them into an IRA (or other qualified account) within 60 calendar days. Limited to one rollover per rolling 12-month period per person (not per IRA, not per calendar year).

cards.front: How does an IRA transfer differ from a rollover?
cards.back: In a transfer (custodian-to-custodian), the customer never takes possession of the assets. There is no limit on the number of transfers per year. Moving 401(k) assets directly to an IRA is technically a transfer (sometimes called a direct rollover).

cards.front: What is the penalty for taking a traditional IRA distribution before age 59½?
cards.back: 10% premature distribution penalty plus ordinary income tax on the distribution.

cards.front: List the exceptions to the 10% premature IRA distribution penalty.
cards.back: Death of the owner, disability of the owner, first-time home purchase (up to $10,000), education expenses for taxpayer/spouse/child/grandchild, medical insurance premiums for the unemployed, and medical expenses above defined AGI limits.

cards.front: At what age must required minimum distributions (RMDs) from a traditional IRA begin?
cards.back: Age 73 (under SECURE 2.0, for individuals reaching age 72 after 12/31/2022). RMDs must be taken by December 31 each year. The first RMD may be delayed until April 1 of the year following the year the owner turns 73, but a second RMD will then be required by December 31 of that same year.

cards.front: A 75-year-old has three traditional IRAs (bank, insurance company, broker-dealer) with combined RMDs totaling $20,000. How may the RMD be satisfied?
cards.back: The full $20,000 may be taken from any one account, or split in any combination across the three accounts, as long as the aggregate $20,000 is withdrawn by the deadline.

cards.front: What is the penalty for failing to take a required minimum distribution (RMD)?
cards.back: Under SECURE 2.0, the penalty is 25% of the shortfall (reduced from the prior 50%), and may be further reduced to 10% if corrected within the correction window.

cards.front: Are Roth IRA contributions tax deductible?
cards.back: No. Roth contributions are made with after-tax dollars and are never deductible. The benefit is tax-free qualified distributions of both contributions and earnings.

cards.front: If the IRA annual contribution limit is $7,000, can a customer contribute $7,000 to a traditional IRA AND $7,000 to a Roth IRA in the same year?
cards.back: No. The limit is a combined cap across ALL of a person's IRAs. The customer could, for example, put $4,000 in the traditional and $3,000 in the Roth — but the total cannot exceed the annual limit.

cards.front: What two conditions must be met for a Roth IRA distribution to be 'qualified' (fully tax free)?
cards.back: (1) The Roth has been open at least 5 years, AND (2) the account holder is at least age 59½. Exceptions to the age requirement: death, disability, or first-time home purchase (up to $10,000).

cards.front: How are nonqualified Roth IRA distributions of earnings taxed?
cards.back: Earnings portions of nonqualified distributions are taxed as ordinary income AND subject to a 10% penalty. Distributions of cost basis (contributions) are always tax free, since they were made with after-tax dollars.

cards.front: Do Roth IRAs require minimum distributions (RMDs)?
cards.back: No. The owner may leave funds in a Roth IRA indefinitely — there is no RMD requirement during the owner's lifetime.

cards.front: For whom is a Roth IRA typically most suitable?
cards.back: Younger investors (more years of tax-free growth), those in lower current tax brackets (the deduction has little value), and anyone unable to deduct traditional IRA contributions due to income or plan coverage.

cards.front: What is the penalty for excess contributions to an IRA?
cards.back: 6% per year on the excess amount, charged every year until the excess is withdrawn.

cards.front: Defined benefit plan
cards.back: An employer-sponsored qualified retirement plan (traditional pension) that defines the benefit a retiree will receive, typically based on years of service, age, and salary. The employer bears the investment risk and must fund the plan to meet the promised payout.

cards.front: Defined contribution plan
cards.back: An employer-sponsored qualified retirement plan that defines what may be contributed (not the final benefit). The employee bears the investment risk; the balance at retirement depends on contributions and investment performance. Examples: 401(k), 403(b), profit-sharing, money purchase, SIMPLE.

cards.front: Joe retires at age 65 after 40 years of service. His employer's pension pays 2% per year of service × average salary of last 5 years ($60,000), capped at 70%. What is Joe's annual benefit?
cards.back: 40 × 2% = 80%, but capped at 70%. 70% × $60,000 = $42,000 per year for life.

cards.front: In a defined benefit pension plan, who bears the investment risk — employer or employee?
cards.back: The employer. The employer must fund the plan adequately to meet the promised benefits, regardless of investment performance. This is a key reason employers have shifted toward defined contribution plans.

cards.front: Name the major types of defined contribution plans.
cards.back: 401(k) plans, 403(b) plans, profit-sharing plans, money purchase plans, and SIMPLE plans.

cards.front: What is purchasing power risk in the context of a private pension?
cards.back: Private pensions pay a fixed benefit that does not change once payments begin, so inflation erodes the purchasing power of the payments. Government pensions often include a cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) to mitigate this.

cards.front: What income type is required to contribute to both a traditional IRA and a Roth IRA in the same year?
cards.back: Earned income. All IRA contributions (traditional or Roth) must be funded from earned income such as wages, salary, or tips — not from passive, portfolio, or ordinary investment income.
